newsitem.title: PERU: Triumphant Fujimori tours bombed-out residence.
newsitem.headline: Triumphant Fujimori tours bombed-out residence.

text.p: With the shirtless body of a dead guerrilla still lying nearby, President Alberto Fujimori on Wednesday toured the Japanese ambassador's home where his elite troops freed 71 hostages from Marxist rebels.
The body of one of the 14 rebels killed in the attack was clearly visible as Fujimori inspected the residence, now pockmarked with holes from explosives.

He walked only a few steps from openings to two tunnels, clearly visible in the garden behind the house, where navy and army troops swept into the building and killed the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels who had held 72 hostages for 126 days.

One hostage, two soldiers and all the captors died -- far fewer than the dozens of deaths earlier predicted by experts and allowing security forces to claim one of the biggest victories in Peru's 17-year war against leftist guerrillas.
The rebels vowed revenge but analysts said the successful raid dealt a devastating blow to the already fading guerrilla group and gave the president a huge political boost.

Fujimori was careful to avoid gloating over the victory. "It could be that it (terrorism) is not defeated. There are still some left, but Peru cannot give in to terrorists' blackmail and Peru should show the international community that terrorism has no impact," he said early on Wednesday.

The MRTA issued a series of blistering statements denying the movement was dead and promising to retaliate by attacking military and economic targets in Peru. Peruvian embassies around the globe were under extra-tight security.

"In the face of the murders of our brothers, we lower our flags in their honour and reaffirm our decision to continue fighting for a society of peace and social justice," said an MRTA statement issued on its Web site.
Police carried out what looked like two body bags from the residence, presumably containing the remains of rebels, some of them teenagers, who died in the surprise attack.
The raid followed months of fruitless negotiations, in which Fujimori went so far as to arrange exile in Cuba for the guerrillas if they released the hostages.
One of three mediators in the talks, Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani, wept at a news conference as he offered condolences to the families of all 17 people who died in the raid.
"The deaths of doctor Giusti, the members of the armed forces and the MRTA hurt me deeply," he said.
Judge Carlos Giusti Acuna, who was wounded and then died after a heart attack, was to be given a formal wake at the Palace of Justice in downtown Lima.

The mediators knew nothing of the raid before it happened, said Cipriani. But he praised Fujimori for making every effort to negotiate an end to the siege, which concluded as violently as it began when MRTA rebels blasted into a pre-Christmas cocktail party hosted by ambassdor Morihisa Aoki.
"I salute President Fujimori. I have seen his enormous patience and effort to achieve a peaceful solution which, in the end, was abandoned," said Cipriani.
The hostages and their loved ones also had surprisingly mixed emotions.

"We're sorry for so much loss of life, the officers, the hostage who died, and for the death among the MRTA, because they're people too," said Father Juan Julio Wicht, a Roman Catholic priest and one of the hostages.
Wicht, speaking to Reuters, said the raid "was nothing like cinema or television" -- and much more terrifying. "I don't know how I got out alive," he said.
He described a miserable life inside the house under MRTA guns, with rats crawling around the hostages as they slept.
"It's marvellous to have my husband back but we feel really deeply the death of Giusti," said Ana Munante, wife of hostage and agriculture minister Rodolfo Munante.
On his first day of freedom, Munante went to his office as usual, "as if everything were all normal again," she said.
The attack was planned after months of spying with microphones and infra-red sensors that gave security forces a precise picture of the inside of the residence.
It was timed to coincide with an indoor soccer game by the rebels, most of whom were teenagers trained in Peru's remote eastern jungle zone.
The soldiers, who had been preparing for months and received training from U.S. and British security experts, began bringing out hostages within minutes.
The rebels originally took 500 hostages but released most in the early days of the crisis, keeping those they considered most valuable to obtain the release of jailed comrades.
